lessonTitle: Clearance, Half-Life and Steady State: Core Pharmacokinetic Parameters and Dosing

blocks.text: A man with atrial fibrillation starts a once-daily drug with a half-life of 36 hours. On day two his blood level is far below the range written in the formulary, yet nothing is wrong. His body has simply not finished accumulating the drug. Knowing why, and how long it takes, is the basis of every dosing regimen.

blocks.markdown: Dosing a drug repeatedly means balancing input against output. Two parameters describe the output side. **Clearance (CL)** is how efficiently the body removes drug, and **volume of distribution (Vd)** is how widely it spreads. From these we derive the **half-life** and the **time to steady state**, then use them to choose a **loading dose** and a **maintenance dose**. This unit assumes first-order (proportional) elimination, which applies to most drugs at therapeutic doses.

blocks.title: Clearance and half-life
blocks.text: Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time (for example L/h). Elimination rate = CL x plasma concentration. Half-life (t1/2) is the time for the plasma concentration to fall by half during elimination. Both CL and Vd are independent determinants; t1/2 is derived from them and is not a fundamental constant of a drug in every patient.

blocks.caption: t1/2 in hours when Vd is in litres and CL in L/h; 0.693 = ln 2. A larger Vd lengthens t1/2 (more drug sits outside the plasma where it cannot be cleared); a larger CL shortens it.

blocks.title: Half-life from clearance and volume of distribution
blocks.prompt: A drug has Vd = 35 L and CL = 5 L/h in a patient (teaching example). Calculate the half-life, and then the half-life if renal impairment halves the clearance with Vd unchanged.

steps.text: Substitute the first set of values.
With renal impairment CL becomes 2.5 L/h.
Halving CL doubled the half-life, so the drug is cleared more slowly and accumulates more with the same dosing.

blocks.answer: About 4.9 h, rising to about 9.7 h when clearance halves

blocks.markdown: **Steady state.** When a drug is given regularly, the amount in the body rises until the rate of elimination equals the rate of input. At that point the average plasma concentration, **Css**, is constant. Because elimination is first order, concentration approaches this plateau exponentially: about 50% of steady state is reached after 1 half-life, 75% after 2, 87.5% after 3, 93.8% after 4 and 96.9% after 5. Steady state is therefore considered reached after about **4 to 5 half-lives**, regardless of dose. Changing the dose changes the final level but not the time taken to reach it.

blocks.caption: Fraction of steady-state concentration reached after repeated dosing with first-order elimination.

blocks.title: Steady state timing
blocks.text: Time to steady state depends only on half-life (about 4 to 5 half-lives), not on dose or frequency. Doubling the maintenance dose doubles Css but does not make steady state arrive sooner.

blocks.caption: Ctarget and Css in mg/L; Vd in L; CL in L/h; F = bioavailability (1 for IV). The loading dose fills the volume of distribution; the maintenance rate replaces drug as fast as it is cleared.

blocks.title: Loading and maintenance dose
blocks.prompt: A drug is to be given by IV infusion to reach a target steady-state concentration of 10 mg/L. Vd = 50 L and CL = 4 L/h (teaching example). Calculate the loading dose and the maintenance infusion rate.

steps.text: For an IV route F = 1. Loading dose = target concentration x Vd.
Maintenance rate must equal elimination rate at the target concentration.

Check the half-life: 0.693 x 50 / 4 = 8.7 h, so without a loading dose steady state would take roughly 35 to 43 h. The loading dose gets the patient to the target immediately, and the maintenance rate then holds it.

blocks.answer: Loading dose 500 mg; maintenance infusion 40 mg/h

items: A loading dose is used when the half-life is long and a rapid effect is needed (for example in arrhythmias or severe infection).
The loading dose depends on Vd (and F), not on clearance.
The maintenance dose depends on CL (and F), not on Vd.
Renal or hepatic impairment lowers CL, so maintenance doses are reduced; the loading dose is usually unchanged.
A dosing interval much longer than t1/2 produces large swings; one much shorter gives smoother levels.

blocks.title: Do not change dose to hurry steady state
blocks.text: If a level is checked before 4 to 5 half-lives, it will be below the eventual Css. Raising the dose because an early level seems low risks toxicity once steady state is reached.

points: Half-life = 0.693 x Vd / CL: it rises when clearance falls or when Vd increases.
Steady state is reached after about 4 to 5 half-lives, independent of dose; dose determines the level, not the time.
Loading dose = target concentration x Vd / F; maintenance rate = CL x Css / F.

questions.stem: Which pair of parameters determines the elimination half-life of a drug with first-order kinetics?

distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: dosing schedule does not alter the half-life.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: bioavailability affects exposure, not half-life.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: peak and trough are outcomes, not determinants.

questions.explanation: Half-life reflects how much drug sits in the body (Vd) relative to how fast it is removed (CL). Dose and schedule change the concentration profile but leave the half-life unchanged.

questions.stem: A drug has a volume of distribution of 60 L and a clearance of 3 L/h. Calculate its half-life in hours, using ln 2 = 0.693.
questions.explanation: t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / CL = 0.693 x 60 / 3 = 0.693 x 20 = 13.86 h. A half-life of this length means dosing once or twice daily is reasonable.

questions.stem: A drug with a half-life of 6 hours is started at a fixed regular dose. Approximately how long in hours will it take to reach steady state, taking 5 half-lives as the standard approximation?
questions.explanation: Steady state is reached after about 4 to 5 half-lives. Taking 5 half-lives gives 5 x 6 h = 30 h, and this is independent of the size of the dose.

questions.stem: A drug is given orally to reach a target plasma concentration of 2 mg/L. Its volume of distribution is 40 L and its oral bioavailability is 0.8. Calculate the loading dose in milligrams. (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: The amount needed in the body is target x Vd = 2 x 40 = 80 mg. Because only 80% of an oral dose reaches the circulation, the dose is divided by F: 80 / 0.8 = 100 mg.

questions.stem: A drug has a clearance of 6 L/h and an oral bioavailability of 0.5. The target average steady-state concentration is 4 mg/L. Calculate the oral maintenance dose in milligrams to be given every 12 hours. (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: Maintenance rate = CL x Css / F = 6 x 4 / 0.5 = 48 mg/h. Over a 12 h interval the dose is 48 x 12 = 576 mg.

questions.stem: A patient is on a stable maintenance dose of a drug and the dose is doubled. What is the expected effect?

options.text: The steady-state concentration doubles but the time to reach steady state is unchanged
The steady-state concentration is unchanged but it is reached twice as fast
The time to steady state doubles and the concentration doubles

questions.correctOptionText: The steady-state concentration doubles but the time to reach steady state is unchanged

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Css is proportional to dose rate; time depends on half-life only.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: dose does not change the time to steady state.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: half-life is independent of dose for first-order drugs.

questions.explanation: Css = dosing rate / CL, so doubling the dose doubles Css. The approach to steady state is governed by the half-life, which has not changed.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman has an estimated glomerular filtration rate that is about half the usual value, and she is started on a drug that is mainly cleared by the kidneys. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Clearance falls, half-life lengthens and steady state takes longer to reach
Volume of distribution doubles and half-life is unchanged
Steady state is reached sooner at a lower level

questions.correctOptionText: Clearance falls, half-life lengthens and steady state takes longer to reach

distractorRationale.a: Correct: t1/2 is inversely proportional to CL, so slower clearance lengthens half-life and delays steady state.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: a lower clearance lengthens, not shortens, half-life.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: Vd is not determined by GFR.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: steady state is later and, without dose reduction, higher.

questions.explanation: Reduced renal function lowers the clearance of a renally cleared drug, and as t1/2 = 0.693 Vd / CL, half-life rises. Steady state then takes longer and, unless the dose is cut, the final concentration is higher.

questions.stem: Which parameter mainly determines the size of a loading dose?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the loading dose fills the volume to the target concentration.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: clearance determines the maintenance dose.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: half-life determines the time to steady state.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: interval does not determine the loading amount.

questions.explanation: Loading dose = target concentration x Vd (divided by F), because the aim is to place the right amount of drug in the body quickly. Clearance only matters afterwards, in replacing drug as it is eliminated.

questions.stem: Explain why a loading dose may be given, how it is calculated, and why the maintenance dose is calculated differently.
markingGuide: Without a loading dose, steady state takes 4 to 5 half-lives, which is too slow for drugs with long half-lives when rapid effect is needed
Loading dose = target concentration x Vd / F, to fill the volume of distribution
Maintenance dose rate = CL x Css / F, to replace drug at the rate it is cleared
Loading dose depends on Vd, maintenance on CL
Worked or stated example with units and a note that renal impairment reduces the maintenance dose but not usually the loading dose
questions.explanation: The two doses serve different purposes: one establishes the target concentration, the other maintains it against elimination. They depend on different parameters, so they are calculated separately.

questions.stem: Describe how the time to reach steady state is estimated after starting regular dosing, and state what determines it.
markingGuide: At steady state input rate equals elimination rate so average concentration is constant
With first-order elimination about 50% of steady state is reached after 1 half-life, 87.5% after 3, about 97% after 5
Steady state therefore takes about 4 to 5 half-lives
Determined by half-life, hence by Vd and CL; not by dose size or frequency
Dose size determines the level reached, so a levels check should wait for steady state
questions.explanation: Because first-order processes approach their endpoint exponentially, each half-life closes half the remaining gap. This gives the practical 4 to 5 half-life rule for steady state.
